chapters.title: Two Ways of Thinking: Hebrew–Eastern and Greek–Western
chapters.subtitle: Why the same Bible can sound different to an Eastern ear and a Western one
chapters.nutshell: The Bible grew up in a Hebrew, Eastern world that thinks in pictures, stories, relationships and community. Much of later Christian theology was shaped in a Greek and Latin world that prizes definitions, systems and the individual. Neither is ‘wrong’, but knowing the difference helps us hear Scripture as its first hearers did.
chapters.bigIdea: Hebrew thought is concrete, relational and communal; Greek–Western thought is abstract, analytical and individual — and the Bible is best read with both eyes open.
skeleton: A helpful generalisation, not an absolute
Hebrew speaks in pictures and actions
Truth, knowing and the person are relational and whole
Community, covenant and history come first
Three culture types: honour–shame, guilt–innocence, fear–power

sections.h: A helpful generalisation, not a wall
p: Scholars often contrast ‘Hebrew’ and ‘Greek’ thinking. This is a helpful generalisation, not an absolute rule. The New Testament itself was written in Greek, Paul quoted Greek poets (Acts 17:28), and many Jews in Jesus’ day already spoke Greek and lived in a Hellenised world. Yet the Bible’s roots, images and assumptions are Hebrew and Eastern, and much later theology was built with Greek and Latin tools (see g-25 and g-07).

Hebrew is a concrete language. It rarely defines God; it pictures him: ‘The LORD is my rock, my fortress’ (Ps 18:2). Anger is a ‘burning nose’, mercy comes from the ‘womb’ (*rechem*), and many key words are verbs of action. Hebrew thinking also holds tensions side by side — God is sovereign and people are responsible (Phil 2:12–13; Acts 2:23). Some call this ‘block logic’: truths are set next to each other rather than forced into a single either–or line.

sections.h: Truth, knowing and the whole person
p: *Emet*, ‘truth’, is first faithfulness — something you can lean on (see s-truth, w-emunah). *Yada*, ‘to know’, is relationship and experience: ‘Adam knew Eve’ (Gen 4:1); to know God is to do justice (Jer 22:16). *Nefesh* is the whole living person, not a soul trapped in a body (see s-soul, s-flesh). In much Western thought, truth became a correct statement, knowing became information, and the person was split into soul and body.

sections.h: We before I; story before system
p: The Bible speaks mostly to a people: ‘Hear, O Israel’. Its faith comes as a story of covenant — promise, rescue, failure, return — moving through real history toward fulfilment in God’s kingdom (see s-kingdom). Western theology has often re-told that story as a system of doctrines and timeless truths, with the individual soul at the centre. Systems are useful, but the Bible’s first form is a family story.

Missionaries often describe three culture types. In honour–shame cultures, the key question is ‘Am I accepted or disgraced before my people?’ In guilt–innocence cultures, it is ‘Have I broken the law?’ In fear–power cultures, it is ‘Am I safe from spirits and powers?’ Every culture has all three; the difference is which leads. The Bible speaks to all three, but its world was mostly honour–shame (see b-life).

If we read only with Western eyes, we may hear the gospel as a courtroom verdict about the afterlife and miss its honour, family, healing and kingdom language (see g-26). If we read only with ‘Eastern’ eyes, we may miss real gains of careful Western study. This section traces how the lens shifted — through Athens, Rome, the Reformation and modern evangelicalism — so we can read with both eyes.

diagrams.title: Six Bible scenes through honour–shame eyes

cards.front: Why is it shocking that the father runs?
cards.back: In the ancient Near East a dignified elder did not run in public. The father gathers his robe, runs, kisses his son and covers his shame before the village sees him.
cards.echo: God takes our shame on himself to restore us.

cards.front: Why does she come at noon?
cards.back: Women usually drew water in the cool of the day. Some readers suggest she came alone to avoid others. Jesus speaks with her publicly, and she becomes a messenger to her town.
cards.echo: Jesus restores honour to the shamed.

cards.front: Why does Jesus stop the crowd?
cards.back: The bleeding woman was ritually unclean and socially cut off. Jesus calls her out publicly, not to shame her, but to name her ‘Daughter’ and restore her place.
cards.echo: Healing includes return to the community.

cards.back: A tax collector was despised. By choosing his house before the whole crowd, Jesus gives him honour first; repentance follows the welcome.

cards.front: Why was the cross a scandal?
cards.back: Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world. Jesus ‘endured the cross, despising the shame’ and turned the place of disgrace into glory.
cards.echo: Salvation as the removal of shame, not only guilt.

cards.back: Peter denied Jesus three times in public. By a charcoal fire, Jesus asks three times ‘Do you love me?’ and publicly gives him back his task.

chapters.title: From Jerusalem to Athens: Greek Philosophy and the Early Church
chapters.subtitle: How Plato’s ideas travelled through Philo, Origen and Augustine into Christian thought
chapters.nutshell: After Alexander the Great, Greek culture filled the eastern Mediterranean. Early Christian thinkers used Greek philosophy to explain and defend the faith, and some of its ideas — the naturally immortal soul, the body as a prison, a God who cannot feel — entered Christian teaching. Yet the church fathers also firmly rejected Gnosticism and held on to creation, incarnation and bodily resurrection.
chapters.bigIdea: Greek philosophy gave the church useful tools but also bent some Hebrew teachings about the body, the soul, God and the future.
skeleton: Philo and the Apologists build bridges
What changed and what held firm

p: From about 332 BC Alexander the Great’s conquests spread Greek language, schools and ideas across the East — a culture called Hellenism. Some Jews resisted it fiercely (the Maccabees, 1 Macc 1–4); others absorbed much of it. The Scriptures were translated into Greek (the Septuagint), and the New Testament was written in Greek. Paul even debated philosophers in Athens (Acts 17:16–34).

Plato (c. 428–348 BC) taught that true reality is the world of eternal, unchanging ‘forms’; the visible world is a shadow. The soul is immortal by nature and existed before birth; the body is its prison — a pun, *sōma sēma*, ‘the body is a tomb’ (Gorgias 493a). Aristotle gave the West its categories and logic, and a God who is the ‘unmoved mover’. The Stoics spoke of a divine Logos (reason) running through all things and prized freedom from passion.

sections.h: Philo and the Apologists: building bridges
p: Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – AD 50), a devout Jew, read the Torah through Plato by allegory: Abraham’s journeys became the soul’s ascent. He spoke of God’s Logos as a go-between. Christian ‘Apologists’ such as Justin Martyr (c. 150) used the Logos as a bridge, saying ‘seeds of the Word’ were scattered among the Greeks. John 1 also speaks of the Logos — but its roots are Genesis 1 and Jewish wisdom, not only Greek thought.

In Alexandria, Clement (c. 150–215) and Origen (c. 185–254) brought philosophy and Scripture together. Origen was a brilliant scholar and a martyr-hearted believer, but he taught that souls existed before bodies and he read much of Scripture as hidden spiritual allegory. Some of his ideas were later condemned (AD 553). Allegory let readers find deep meanings, but it could also float free from the Bible’s history and story.

Augustine (354–430) says that ‘books of the Platonists’ — Neoplatonism, from Plotinus (c. 204–270) — helped him think of God as spiritual and unchanging (Confessions 7). His towering influence shaped Western teaching on grace, sin and the afterlife (see g-38, g-39). His view of original sin leaned on the Latin of Romans 5:12, *in quo omnes peccaverunt*, ‘in whom (Adam) all sinned’; the Greek *eph’ hō* is usually read today as ‘because all sinned’.

sections.h: What changed — and what held firm
p: Greek influence pressed toward a God who cannot suffer or change (impassibility, immutability), while the Hebrew Bible shows a God who grieves (Gen 6:6), relents (Jonah 3:10) and whose heart is moved (Hos 11:8). It encouraged suspicion of the body and hope of heaven as escape rather than new creation (Rom 8:19–23; Rev 21). Yet the fathers, such as Irenaeus, fought Gnosticism (see g-33), affirmed that creation is good, that God became flesh, and that the body will rise.

chapters.title: Rome and Latin: Law, Empire and the Church
chapters.subtitle: How a Jewish family of faith became an imperial institution with a legal vocabulary
chapters.nutshell: In the Latin-speaking West, the faith was explained in the language of Roman law: satisfaction, merit, penance. When Constantine embraced Christianity, the church gained freedom and power, separated itself from its Jewish roots, and began to mirror the empire’s structures. By the Middle Ages this produced a system of merit, purgatory and indulgences that the Reformation would challenge.
chapters.bigIdea: Latin law and Roman empire gave the Western church its vocabulary and its structure — and narrowed some biblical ideas along the way.
skeleton: The Latin West and the Greek East

p: The Roman Empire spoke two main languages: Greek in the East and Latin in the West (Rome, North Africa, Gaul, Spain). Eastern churches also spoke Syriac, Coptic and Armenian. Over the centuries the Latin West developed its own style: practical, legal and organised. The Greek East stayed more mystical and liturgical. The split became formal in 1054.

Tertullian of Carthage (c. 160–220) was the first great Christian writer in Latin. He asked, ‘What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?’ — yet he brought Roman legal words into theology: *satisfactio* (making amends), *meritum* (merit), *persona* (a legal person) and *trinitas* (Trinity). Whether he was trained as a lawyer is debated, but his thinking is legal in tone. These words were useful, but they could turn a covenant relationship into a court case.

Jerome’s Vulgate (c. 382–405) became the Bible of the West for a thousand years. It rendered Greek *metanoia* (‘a change of mind and direction’) with *paenitentia*, and ‘repent’ as *paenitentiam agite*, later understood as ‘do penance’. *Dikaioō* became *iustificare*, ‘to make righteous’, shaping medieval teaching on justification (see s-justify, t-translation). Jerome was a careful scholar; Latin simply could not carry every Hebrew and Greek nuance.

In 313 the Edict of Milan gave Christians freedom. Constantine made Sunday a day of rest by law (321) and called the Council of Nicaea (325), which also set Easter apart from the Jewish Passover reckoning. In 380 Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the state religion. Persecution ended — a real mercy — but the church gained wealth, buildings and political power, and bishops began to resemble imperial officials.

Church and synagogue separated gradually over the first centuries; scholars debate when and how. Sadly, a whole genre of writings ‘against the Jews’ (*adversus Iudaeos*) grew up, and Jews were blamed collectively for Jesus’ death. Imperial laws later restricted Jews. The faith that began as a Jewish movement (see g-07) increasingly defined itself against Israel — a tragedy with long and bitter consequences.

sections.h: Anselm, merit and the medieval system
p: Around 1098 Anselm of Canterbury wrote *Cur Deus Homo* (‘Why God Became Man’): sin offends God’s honour, and only the God-man can pay the satisfaction owed — a picture drawn from feudal society (see g-17). Medieval teaching added merit, penance, purgatory and indulgences, which could reduce time in purgatory. When indulgences were sold to raise money, Luther protested in 1517.

chapters.title: Reformation and Enlightenment: Text, Self and Reason
chapters.subtitle: How the printed Bible, the lone conscience and the thinking self reshaped faith
chapters.nutshell: The printing press put the Bible into ordinary hands, and the Reformers recovered the free grace of God — a real gain. But the Reformation and the Enlightenment also moved the centre of faith toward the individual, the text and reason. Faith could become agreement with correct statements, and religion a private matter.
chapters.bigIdea: The Reformation recovered grace and Scripture, while the Enlightenment made the individual mind the starting point — and both shaped how the West reads the Bible.
skeleton: The printing press and the open Bible
Descartes and Locke: self and reason
The Bible as a book of doctrines

sections.h: The printing press and the open Bible
p: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg’s printing press began a revolution; his Bible appeared about 1455. Within a century Bibles, tracts and catechisms spread in the languages of the people. Ordinary believers could read Scripture for themselves — a huge blessing. But faith also became more a matter of private reading and printed doctrine than of shared memory, story and worship.

Martin Luther (1483–1546) rediscovered that we are put right with God by grace through faith, not by buying merit: *sola gratia*, *sola fide*, *sola scriptura*. This recovered a true biblical emphasis (Rom 3:24; Eph 2:8–9). Debate continues over his ‘forensic’ view — that justification is mainly a legal declaration — and how it relates to covenant and transformation (see s-justify). John Calvin’s *Institutes* (1536; final edition 1559) set out the faith as a clear, ordered system.

Luther’s stand at Worms (1521) became a symbol of the individual conscience bound to Scripture. The following century produced detailed confessions and ‘Protestant scholasticism’, which defined doctrine with logical precision. This gave clarity and protected against error. But it also tended to make the Christian life a matter of holding the right system — and the individual, rather than the people of God, became the main unit of faith.

sections.h: Descartes and Locke: the self and reason
p: In 1637 René Descartes wrote, ‘I think, therefore I am’. Certainty now began from the thinking self. John Locke (1632–1704) argued that faith must be reasonable and treated belief as assent to propositions supported by evidence. Deists went further: God made the world like a clock and stepped back. Religion was increasingly seen as private opinion, separate from public life — the sacred–secular split.

sections.h: The Bible as a book of doctrines
p: In this climate the Bible was often read as a storehouse of true statements and proof texts to be arranged into a system. Verses were lifted from their story and setting. Yet the Bible is first the story of Israel fulfilled in Jesus, and biblical faith (*emunah*) is faithful trust, not only mental agreement (see w-emunah, s-truth). The Reformers themselves insisted that true faith includes heartfelt trust (*fiducia*).

From the 18th century, modern biblical criticism studied Scripture like any ancient text, questioning authorship and history. Some of its tools — language, archaeology, careful history — have helped us greatly; some conclusions undermined trust in the Bible. Many believers reacted by defending the Bible’s accuracy point by point. Some historians observe that both sides often shared the same modern assumption: that the Bible’s value lies chiefly in factual propositions (see e-evangelical).

quiz.why: Luther rediscovered free grace (Eph 2:8–9) — a real gain.

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word *emunah* mean?

options: Belief in a distant God who does not intervene
quiz.why: Deists pictured God as a clockmaker who stepped back from the world.

terms.def: ‘Scripture alone’ as the final authority for faith.
‘Faith alone’: justification by faith, not by merit.
Justification understood mainly as a legal declaration of righteousness.
17th-century Protestant theology using precise logical definitions.
Belief in a creator who does not act in the world.
Dividing life into religious and non-religious zones.
